metadata.transcript:
TUTOR: Right, thanks for sending through the draft proposal — I've had a good read of it. Overall it's a promising start, but there are a couple of things to think about before you take it further. So, my first thought: the proposal sets out to investigate the impact of part-time work on academic performance — which is fine — but the question you're asking is really very wide. You're trying to cover every kind of student across the whole university, and I'm not sure that's manageable in one term.

STUDENT 2: Yes, we wondered about that.

TUTOR: And the other thing — the one I'd flag most strongly — is how you'll measure academic performance. Right now you're relying on students telling you their own grades, which isn't the most reliable source — people tend to round up. Your sample of two hundred is perfectly adequate, mind, and the timeline looks realistic, so it's really those two issues.

STUDENT 1: Right. So for the first one — the breadth — what if we looked at just one department, rather than the whole institution? The Business students, say, since that's where most part-time workers are.

TUTOR: That would help enormously, yes.

STUDENT 2: And for the grades — could we ask the department to give us the actual results directly?

TUTOR: You could certainly ask. The registry can release anonymised data with the right permissions, so that's the route I'd take rather than self-reported figures.

STUDENT 1: Should we run a pilot first?

TUTOR: You could, but with the time you've got, I wouldn't bother.

STUDENT 2: And what about the rest of it?

TUTOR: Well, honestly, the part that stood out was your review of the earlier studies. It's thorough, it's critical, and it sets your own work up nicely — that's the section an examiner would be most impressed by. The analysis plan is fine, and the topic, while interesting, isn't especially new.

STUDENT 1: Good to know. So for the design, we'll compare students working longer hours with those doing less.

TUTOR: Yes, you'll want a clear cut-off. I'd say the dividing line should be more than fifteen hours a week — not ten, that's too low to show an effect, and twenty would leave too few students in the group.

STUDENT 2: Right, that makes sense. And for the performance data, we'll use their end-of-semester results, so we're comparing the same point for everyone.

TUTOR: Good. And remember, since you're handling personal data, every response must be kept anonymous — no names anywhere in the dataset.

STUDENT 1: Understood. We were also thinking of presenting the early results at the department seminar in March.

TUTOR: Nice idea. One last thing — when you write it up, include a proper section on the limitations of the study. Examiners always look for that.

STUDENT 2: Will do. Thanks.

TUTOR: Good. Send me the revised version next week.
